---
title: 'Logarithmic Spiral ($e^x$)'
format: html
code-fold: True
---

When a young fern sprout (known as a fiddlehead) is tightly coiled, it forms a logarithmic spiral.

![Logarithmic spiral in fiddlehead](figures/Spiral-Fiddlehead.jpeg){width="2.6in" fig-pos="H"}


Logarithmic spiral spiral appears often in nature such as:

* nautilus shell,
* hurricane,
* spiral galaxies.  

![Logarithmic spiral in Nautilus Shell](figures/Spiral-Nautilus.png){width="2.6in" fig-pos="H"}
![Logarithmic spiral in Hurricane](figures/Spiral-Hurricane.jpg){width="2.3in" fig-pos="H"}
![Logarithmic spiral in Spiral Galaxies](figures/Spiral-Galaxies.jpg){width="2.8in" fig-pos="H"}

One of characteristic properties of logarithmic spiral is complete self-similarity. If you shrink or enlarge it by any arbitrary scale factor, not just a specific fixed ratio, and rotate it by an appropriat angle, it matches the original spiral. 

![Logarithmic spiral is completely self-similar](figures/Spiral-Self-Similarity.png){width="6in" fig-pos="H"}
